key_concept: Radial symmetry means any plane through the central axis gives two identical halves; echinoderm adults are radially symmetrical but their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
steps: Statement I: In radial symmetry, any plane passing through the central (oral–aboral) axis divides the body into two identical halves. Examples are coelenterates, ctenophores and adult echinoderms. This is the standard definition, so Statement I is correct.
Statement II: Adult echinoderms, such as the starfish, show radial symmetry, usually pentamerous (five-part).
Echinoderm larvae, such as the bipinnaria of the starfish, are bilaterally symmetrical. Only one plane divides them into identical left and right halves.
Bilateral larvae with radial adults show that echinoderms evolved from bilateral ancestors, and their radial symmetry is secondary.
Because the larvae are not radially symmetrical, Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect, so the answer is Option (3).
final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) accept Statement II, but echinoderm larvae are bilateral, not radial. Option (2) wrongly rejects Statement I, which is the textbook definition of radial symmetry.
common_trap: Students extend the radial symmetry of adult echinoderms to their larvae, forgetting that the larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
time_saving_tip: Remember the one-liner: Echinodermata have radial adults and bilateral larvae. Any statement claiming both stages are radial is false.
